column2: Behold introduces the report of foreigners fighting at Keilah, plundering and trampling threshing floors. Both destructive actions remain.
David inquires through the Lord about striking; the reply commands going and predicts striking and saving Keilah. The city's rescue remains the action's stated outcome.
The men present current fear in Judea, question a move to Keilah and speak of entering the foreigners' spoils. The selected spoils expression is not replaced by battle lines.
column3: The final prediction is unusual and remains provisional; no missing object or alternative reading is reconstructed.

column2: David inquires again, and the repeated reply commands descent because the Lord is handing the foreigners into his hands. Again follows the explicit repetition.
Travel, battle, enemy flight, livestock removal, a great blow and rescue of Keilah's inhabitants all remain. The explicit flight clause is not omitted.
Abiathar son of Abimelech descends with David to Keilah while carrying the ephoud in his hand; the selected movement and named father remain.
Saul interprets the report as God selling David into his hands because a barred and gated city shuts him in. The divine-sale claim remains Saul's own interpretation.
Saul mobilizes all the people for war and descent to hem in David and his men; the enclosure purpose is not reduced to a general visit.
David knows Saul is not silent about the evil concerning him and requests the Lord's ephoud from Abiathar. The selected lack-of-silence wording is retained.
Propose surely heard for the emphatic hearing construction in David's prayer. Thy servant retains direct singular divine address, with Saul's intended destruction of Keilah because of David explicit.
The shut-up question, Saul's possible descent, repeated divine address and request to tell Thy servant precede the Lord's It will be shut up answer.
column3: The passive's subject is unstated and unresolved; no object or Keilahite surrender question is invented. Missing label 12 is preserved.

column2: About four hundred depart Keilah, go wherever they go and cause Saul to abandon his expedition when escape is reported. The selected four hundred is not changed to six hundred.
Maserem's narrow places, wilderness, Mount Ziph and parched land remain, with Saul's daily pursuit and the Lord's refusal to hand David over.
David sees Saul going out to seek David, and the narrative locates David on the parched mountain at Kaine of Ziph; repeated naming remains.
Jonathan, explicitly Saul's son, comes to Kaine and strengthens David's hands in the Lord. The bodily support image is not reduced to generic encouragement.
Propose For before the reason not to fear. Saul's hand certainly not finding David, David's future reign, Jonathan's second place and Saul's knowledge remain as Jonathan's assurances.
Both men covenant before the Lord, then David remains at Kaine while Jonathan returns home. Their divergent movements remain.
The Ziphites' ascent from parched land and their presentative question retain Messara, narrow places, Kaine, Echela and the right of Jessaimoun.
column3: The location chain is preserved without equating every name with a later or Hebrew toponym.

column2: The king is invited to descend according to his soul's whole desire, and an unnamed plural they have shut David into his hands remains.
column3: The plural actor of shut is not silently changed to we will surrender; the tense and agency are left as selected.

column2: Saul blesses the informants by the Lord because they took trouble for him; the blessing remains his speech, not narrator approval.
Going, further preparation, knowing the foot's place, quickly, where previously stated, and the fear of cunning remain in the compressed command.
column3: The attachment of quickly and where you said is unsettled; the inherited order does not claim a resolved map or a distinct scouting action absent from the text.

column2: Seeing and knowing precede the shared expedition and Saul's conditional search among Judah's thousands; no specific clan census is inferred.
The Ziphites precede Saul while David's group occupies Maan's wilderness westward/right of Jessaimoun; the directional wording is not replaced by a familiar geographic formula.
column3: Westward for kath hesperan is the geographic construal; evening is a lexical possibility requiring contextual review.

column2: Saul's search prompts an unnamed report to David, descent to the rock and Saul's renewed pursuit into Maan; reporting agents remain unspecified.
Both groups are located along a side of this mountain; David keeps covered to leave, while Saul's men camp against his group to capture them.
column3: The repeated side wording is retained without adding one side/the other as if explicitly distinct Greek terms; covering and pursuit geometry remain interpretive.

column2: The messenger's hurry-and-come commands are grounded in foreigners attacking the land; the emergency interrupts the pursuit without a new battle outcome.
Saul ceases pursuing David and goes to meet the foreigners, explaining the Divided Rock name. The selected translated name remains.
David's ascent and residence in En-gedi's narrow places begin chapter 24 in the selected numbering; no move to the preceding chapter is made.
Saul's return from the foreigners precedes the report locating David in En-gedi's wilderness; the repeated location remains.
Three thousand chosen men from all Israel accompany the search in front of Sadaiem. The selected name is not changed to a wild-goat description.
Flocks' herds beside the road, a cave, Saul's attending to himself and David's group farther inside remain.
column3: Attend to himself renders paraskeuasasthai cautiously; the precise activity and unusual herd phrase are not expanded into an unexpressed bodily description.

column2: The men interpret the day as promised divine delivery and permission to act as good in David's eyes, while David secretly removes Saul's double-cloak flap. Their interpretation is not converted into a new narrator prophecy.
David's heart strikes him after the removal; the bodily conscience image and repeated cloak flap remain.

The negative oath rejects bringing David's hand against his human lord, twice identified as the Lord's anointed. The inherited May the Lord forbid expresses the oath without changing the addressee to God.
David persuades with words and prevents rising to kill, while Saul rises and descends to the road. The two rising actions remain distinct.
David emerges behind Saul, calls Lord king and bows face to ground after Saul looks back. The human title is sentence-initial capitalized, not a divine-pronoun decision.
David questions listening to people who claim he seeks Saul's soul, preserving their Behold inside the quotation.
Behold introduces the day's visible delivery in the cave, David's unwillingness to kill and sparing, and his quoted refusal to strike the anointed. The repeated today language remains.
The displayed cloak flap proves removal without killing; David urges knowing and seeing no evil, impiety or rejection, denies sin and accuses Saul of binding his soul to take it.
column3: Rejection for athetesis remains provisional in the charge list; binding is not replaced by a more familiar hunting image.

column2: The optative appeal asks divine judgment and vengeance while firmly excluding David's own hand against Saul. The distinction of divine and human agency remains.
The ancient proverb links wrongdoing to the lawless, followed by the repeated refusal of David's hand against Saul; the maxim is not embellished into a wider moral rule.
Two pursuit questions address Israel's king, then name a dead dog and one flea. Dead and single are explicit and retained.
The Lord is invoked as judge and arbiter, asked to see, judge David's case and give judgment from Saul's hand; the clustered legal verbs remain.
After David's speech, Saul recognizes child David's voice, raises his own voice and weeps. The affectionate title and audible reaction remain.
Saul acknowledges greater righteousness and contrasts David's good repayment with his own evil repayment; both first- and second-person agencies remain.
Saul speaks of today's report, the good done, the Lord's shutting him into David's hands and David's non-killing. Shutting is retained as his stated divine action.
Propose For at the explanatory conditional. Finding an enemy in distress and releasing him on a good road leads to the Lord's future good repayment, compared with David's act today.
column3: The selected affirmative conditional is not replaced by a rhetorical question that an enemy would never be released.

column2: Now behold introduces Saul's knowledge of David's certain reign and establishment of Israel's kingdom in his hands; surely renders the cognate reigning emphasis.
Saul requests an oath against destruction of his seed and disappearance of his name from his father's house; both protected continuities remain.
David swears, Saul returns to his place and David's company ascends to narrow Messara. The selected place form and separate departures remain.
